# The working life of Raijin: from the myths to the modern trades

The myths did not retire. They moved offices. This is the file on where **Raijin** works now.

Raijin's mythology is a palimpsest: the thunder kami of the Kojiki, the Buddhist guardian of esoteric temple art, the storm god of the Mongol-invasion legend, and the bogey of nursery warnings — four layers of one drumbeat. The sources are layered and partly at odds, and each layer tells us what thunder meant to a different Japan.

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) — which maps every flagship temple to the industries its archetype demonstrably resonates with, each match argued and open to challenge — seats this temple in **3 industries**. This file reads those seats the way they were earned: through the myths.

## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Raijin
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Domain of influence:** Thunder, Lightning
- **Pattern seats:** 3
- **Sectors touched:** Culture & Entertainment · Energy & Natural World · Commerce & Governance
- **Strongest seat:** Music, Arts & Performance
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 410 of 546

## The Myth at Work

**Thunder Born of the Dead Goddess.** In the Kojiki, Izanami dies from the burns of the fire god Kagutsuchi, and her grieving husband Izanagi pursues her into Yomi, the land of the dead.  When he breaks his promise not to look, he sees her body corrupted; in her fury Izanami sends the yakusa no ikazuchi — the eight thunder spirits — in pursuit, together with the hags of Yomi. — hold that image; the industries below are where it goes to work.

**Guardian of the Dharma.** With the arrival of esoteric Buddhism, the thunder power was enrolled in the defenses of the Dharma.  From the Heian period, Raijin appears among the Jūni-ten, the Twelve Devas who guard the four directions and the zenith and nadir of the mandala, and with Fūjin he comes to stand at temple gatehouses — the pair most famously at the great Nioh-mon gates of Zen temples, where their sculpted forms confront visitors with the storm itself. — hold that image; the industries below are where it goes to work.

## The Seats

Each of these is argued in the atlas with a weight and a why-line. What the atlas cannot fit in one line is the whole myth — so here is each seat with its story restored.

### Music, Arts & Performance

*Music, theatre, dance, and the performing arts. (Sector: Culture & Entertainment)*

*The thunder kami whose taiko drums circle every storm; Sōtatsu's Fūjin-Raijin screens are national treasures.* — the atlas stops there, out of discipline. The myth keeps going: the function Raijin performs in the stories is precisely the function this industry sells.

### Meteorology & Weather Intelligence

*Forecasting, storm tracking, and climate analytics. (Sector: Energy & Natural World)*

*The thunder kami who beats his drums around the storm; Japanese art pairs him with Fūjin as the weather itself.* — the atlas stops there, out of discipline. The myth keeps going: the function Raijin performs in the stories is precisely the function this industry sells.

### Insurance & Protection Services

*Insurance, assurance, and risk protection. (Sector: Commerce & Governance)*

*Thunder and lightning are the oldest insurable risks; his drums are the claim siren.* — the atlas stops there, out of discipline. The myth keeps going: the function Raijin performs in the stories is precisely the function this industry sells.

## The Long Employment

Raijin remains one of Japan's most visually striking deities.  His most famous portrait, Tawaraya Sōtatsu's Fūjin-Raijin-zu screens (early seventeenth century, now a National Treasure at Kennin-ji in Kyoto), is a canonical image of Japanese art, endlessly reproduced. The age changed. The work did not.

## The Method, Stated Plainly
